guide_line: Tell a hypothesis, a law, and a theory apart, and name the domain.
steps: Chemistry studies what matter is made of and how it changes.
A hypothesis is a testable guess. A law states a pattern that keeps happening. A theory explains a pattern after many tests.
Macroscopic is what you can see or measure. Microscopic is atoms and molecules. Symbolic is formulas, symbols, and equations.

worked_example.q: A student watches ice melt into liquid water. Which domain is that observation?
steps: The student is watching a change that can be seen.
The observation does not use a formula or a picture of atoms.

similar_problem.q: A page shows the formula H2O for water. Which domain is the formula?
similar_problem.hint: H2O is a written symbol for water, not the water you can pour.

problems.q: Classify the statement: every sample of pure water boils at the same temperature when the pressure is the same.
problems.why: The statement reports a pattern that repeats. It does not give a cause, so it is a law.
hints: This sentence only says what always happens to pure water. It does not say why.

problems.q: Classify the statement: the metal strip may bend because the two metals expand by different amounts.
problems.why: "May" marks a cause you could test. A testable guess is a hypothesis.
hints: Look for a proposed cause of the bend that an experiment could check.

problems.q: Classify the statement: many experiments support the idea that matter is made of atoms, and that idea explains why a compound has a fixed recipe.
problems.why: The atom idea explains a pattern and has passed many tests. That is a theory.
hints: This claim both explains a pattern and says it has already survived many experiments.

problems.q: You see a blue liquid in a beaker. Which domain is that observation?
problems.why: The color and the beaker are things you can see. That is the macroscopic domain.
hints: The blue liquid and the beaker are visible. No formula is required.

problems.q: A sketch shows separate H2 molecules and O2 molecules. Which domain is the sketch?
problems.why: Molecules are too small to see. A picture of them is the microscopic domain.
hints: The sketch is about molecules, which you cannot see with your eyes.

problems.q: The board shows the equation 2 H2 + O2 → 2 H2O. Which domain is the equation?
problems.why: An equation is written with symbols. That is the symbolic domain.
hints: An equation uses symbols and numbers, not a photo of the reaction.

problems.q: Classify the statement: I think the fizz is a gas made by the reaction.
problems.why: "I think" offers a cause that a test could support or reject. That is a hypothesis.
hints: The speaker is guessing the source of the fizz before a test is done.

problems.q: Classify the statement: heating a gas in a sealed tube always raises its pressure.
problems.why: "Always" reports a repeated pattern and gives no explanation. That is a law.
hints: The sentence says the pressure rise happens every time. It never says why.

problems.q: Name the three domains: the visible world, the atom-level world, and the world of formulas.
problems.why: Visible samples are macroscopic. Atoms and molecules are microscopic. Formulas and equations are symbolic.
hints: Match each phrase in the question to one domain name, in any order.

nearMiss.hint: Submicroscopic is another label for the atom-level view. This lesson uses microscopic.

problems.q: A balance reads 2.50 g. Which domain is that reading?
problems.why: A balance reading is a lab measurement you can make directly. That is macroscopic.
hints: A balance reading is a measurement of a sample you can handle.

problems.q: A bottle label shows the symbol Na. Which domain is the symbol?
problems.why: Na is a chemical symbol, not the metal itself. Symbols are the symbolic domain.
hints: Na stands for the metal. The letters are not the shiny piece of metal.

problems.q: A model shows Na+ and Cl− ions packed in a crystal. Which domain is the model?
problems.why: Ions in a crystal are too small to see. The model is microscopic.
hints: The model shows ions, which are far too small to see in the crystal.
